ENT Clinical Note – Video Consultation

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: Activity-related right-sided (occasional bilateral) knee pain with clicking after increasing running mileage for marathon training.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Began ~2 weeks ago; pain starts ≈20 min / 2.5–3 mi into run, worsened with continued running and some gym leg-extension/ab exercises. Occasional transient mild swelling after first long run (responded to ice). One episode of right-toe tingling post-run. No constant/rest pain.
- ENT symptoms: 
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation – Denied  
  • Voice change/hoarseness – Denied  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia – Denied  
  • Drooling – Denied  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms – Denied  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing – Denied  
  • Dyspnea – Denied  
  • Swelling of lips/tongue/uvula/face – Denied  
  • Ear pain/hearing change – Denied  
  • Neck pain/swelling – Denied
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: Remote right knee contusion from ice-hockey fall months ago; resolved. Used ice and PRN ibuprofen (400 mg) with relief. No prior injections, ED visits, or surgeries for knee or ENT issues.
- Allergies: Not documented (none stated).
- Current medications: Ibuprofen 400 mg PO PRN; Aleve (naproxen) PRN – dose/frequency not documented; vitamin D – dose not documented; melatonin – dose not documented; occasional Xanax – dose not documented; occasional cannabis joint.
- Social context: Lives independently; highly physically active; training for marathon.

Objective:
- Observable swelling/distribution: Patient reports no current knee swelling; no facial/oropharyngeal swelling.
- Airway/breathing: No distress, stridor, or dyspnea reported or observed.
- Mental status/associated features: Alert, oriented; no dizziness or syncope reported.
- Vitals & physical examination: Not recorded (video consultation only; patient reports full knee flexion/extension, no locking, no giving-way).
- Presence of companion: Not mentioned.

Assessment:
- Working impression: Overuse-related right knee pain, most consistent with patellofemoral pain syndrome; no evidence of ENT or airway involvement.
  Evidence: Pain provoked by running/leg-extension, onset with mileage increase, clicking, full ROM, absence of instability, swelling minimal and transient.
- DDx (from reasoning system, aligned with transcript):
  1. Patellofemoral pain syndrome – high likelihood; classic activity-related anterior/central knee pain with clicking, normal exam.
  2. Patellar tendinopathy – medium likelihood; overuse of extensor mechanism, activity-linked pain.
  3. Meniscal tear – medium likelihood; prior trauma and clicking support; opposing evidence: no locking or persistent effusion.
  (No ENT pathologies suggested; transcript/DDx consistent.)

Plan:
- Immediate management:
  • Continue regular ice application after activity.  
  • Prescribed stronger oral NSAID (exact agent/dose per e-prescription) to be taken with food; avoid concurrent ibuprofen.  
  • Advise relative rest: reduce running mileage; stop activity if pain forces cessation.
- Referrals / follow-up:
  • Physiotherapy referral for detailed knee assessment and rehabilitation programme.  
  • Consider in-clinic review and/or imaging if physiotherapy wait is prolonged or if symptoms escalate.
- Patient instructions & red-flags:
  • Return/call urgently for persistent or worsening knee swelling, redness, heat, fever, locking, inability to bear weight, or new neurologic symptoms.  
  • Monitor medication tolerance; stop NSAID and seek care for gastric pain, melena, or allergic reaction.
- Avoidance/education: Gradual training progression; proper footwear; warm-up/cool-down.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing/expected elements: Formal allergy list; vital signs; detailed knee physical exam findings (inspection, palpation, patellar tracking); medication dose/frequency for naproxen, vitamin D, melatonin, Xanax; documentation of smoking/alcohol status; ENT-specific exam not performed (no indication).  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear, minimal background noise; no inaudible segments.
